content: The establishment of baseline data for tuberculosis (TB) cases has not yet been finalized. However, in 2011, a survey was conducted on a nationally representative sample of previously untreated TB cases, following the recommendations of the World Health Organization (WHO). A total of 78 study sites across the country were selected using a probability proportional to size approach. All consecutive new pulmonary TB cases presenting at 39 selected health centers were enrolled in the study. Culture and drug sensitivity results were available for 1,050 out of the 1,080 enrolled patients, meeting the second benchmark for data completeness. The WHO recommends that all patients with suspected or diagnosed TB undergo HIV testing and counseling to ensure early detection and prompt initiation of treatment. This recommendation applies regardless of the HIV epidemic state, whether generalized, concentrated, or low-level. In settings with a low-level HIV epidemic, where routine HIV testing for most TB cases is not feasible, data collection can be achieved through periodic surveys of a sample of TB cases. When routine surveillance systems are used to assess the representativeness of HIV testing results, it is essential that at least 80% of all notified TB cases have their HIV status documented. Routine HIV testing and counseling provide significant benefits for individuals living with HIV, including improved access to testing, early case detection, and rapid initiation of treatment. In countries with separate systems for TB and HIV surveillance, where confidentiality or other reasons prevent routine documentation of HIV status in the TB surveillance system, record linkage between the two systems should be performed to assess whether benchmarks have been met. In settings where routine surveillance is not feasible, periodic or sentinel surveys are recommended every 2–3 years, in line with WHO policies on collaborative TB/HIV activities. The main limitations include the existence of separate TB and HIV surveillance systems in some countries, which complicates record linkage. This process can be time-consuming and complex, especially in settings where unique patient identifiers are not routinely used. Legal restrictions may also prevent record linkage, making periodic surveys a suitable alternative. The standard is considered met if 80% or more of TB cases have a documented HIV status. If HIV status is documented for 50–79% of cases or if a periodic HIV survey is underway, the standard is partially met. If neither benchmark is satisfied, the standard is not met. In countries with a generalized HIV epidemic, such as Kenya and South Africa, significant progress has been made in integrating HIV testing and antiretroviral therapy (ART) into TB care. For example, in Kenya, over 80% of TB patients had their HIV status recorded in 2011, demonstrating the success of collaborative TB/HIV activities. Similarly, in South Africa, 83% of TB cases had a known HIV status recorded in the TB register in 2011. These achievements highlight the importance of integrating HIV testing and treatment into TB care to improve outcomes for co-infected patients. The diagnosis of TB in children remains a significant challenge due to difficulties in obtaining sputum specimens and the reliance on clinical criteria and diagnostic tests. In high TB endemic settings, most childhood TB cases occur in young children with paucibacillary disease, which is harder to diagnose. The emphasis on sputum smear-positive cases in national TB program (NTP) reporting has led to underdiagnosis and underreporting of childhood TB. This, combined with the lack of routine recording and reporting of childhood TB, results in an underestimation of the true burden of the disease in children. To address these challenges, NTPs should assess the level of underreporting of childhood TB cases through inventory studies conducted within the past 10 years. If no recent inventory studies have been conducted, planning for such a study should begin, following WHO guidelines. If a large proportion of diagnosed cases go unreported, urgent action is needed to identify and address the reasons for underreporting. Corrective actions, such as training and strengthening monitoring and evaluation systems, may be required to improve the accuracy and completeness of TB surveillance data. The registration of TB cases should be completed using standardized recording and reporting formats, collecting patient demographic, clinical, diagnostic, and treatment outcome data. Basic management units (BMUs) for TB control should oversee TB activities, maintain a master register of all TB patients, and monitor program performance. The BMU TB register should include all diagnosed TB cases eligible for treatment, including those with rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB, regardless of whether treatment was initiated. These cases should be included in summary case notification reports sent to higher levels. In summary, achieving high coverage of HIV surveillance among TB patients and addressing the challenges of diagnosing and reporting childhood TB are critical for improving TB control efforts. Collaborative TB/HIV activities, periodic surveys, and inventory studies are essential tools for understanding and addressing the dual TB/HIV epidemic and ensuring accurate and comprehensive surveillance data.
